elements.name: Hydrogen
elements.note: The lightest element and the most common in the universe; with oxygen it makes water.

elements.name: Helium
elements.note: A noble gas that reacts with almost nothing; it lifts balloons and cools scanner magnets.

elements.name: Lithium
elements.note: The lightest metal; it powers rechargeable batteries.

elements.name: Beryllium
elements.note: A light, stiff metal used in aircraft parts and X-ray windows.

elements.name: Boron
elements.note: A metalloid used in glass, soaps, and heat-proof cookware.

elements.name: Carbon
elements.note: The backbone of living things; diamond, graphite, coal, and oil are all carbon.

elements.name: Nitrogen
elements.note: About 78 parts in 100 of the air; it keeps food fresh in sealed bags.

elements.name: Oxygen
elements.note: About 21 parts in 100 of the air; fires burn and lungs breathe because of it.

elements.name: Fluorine
elements.note: The most reactive element; it protects teeth in tiny amounts.

elements.name: Neon
elements.note: A noble gas that lights signs in bright red-orange.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.note: A soft metal that joins with chlorine to make common salt.

elements.name: Magnesium
elements.note: A light metal that burns with a bright white light; it feeds plants as chlorophyll's heart.

elements.name: Aluminium
elements.note: A light, strong metal used in aircraft, cans, and window frames.

elements.name: Silicon
elements.note: The heart of computer chips and solar cells; sand and glass are mostly silicon.

elements.name: Phosphorus
elements.note: Used in fertilisers, matches, and fireworks; it glows in the dark.

elements.name: Sulfur
elements.note: The yellow element of matches, gunpowder, and volcanic fumes.

elements.name: Chlorine
elements.note: A sharp green gas that cleans water and makes salt with sodium.

elements.name: Argon
elements.note: A noble gas that fills light bulbs and welds metal without reacting.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.note: A metal the body needs for nerves and muscles; it feeds plants as potash.

elements.name: Calcium
elements.note: The metal of bones, teeth, milk, and chalk.

elements.name: Scandium
elements.note: A light metal used in aircraft parts and bicycle frames.

elements.name: Titanium
elements.note: A strong, light, rust-proof metal used in aircraft, implants, and paint.

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.note: A hard metal used in steel tools and springs.

elements.name: Chromium
elements.note: The metal that keeps steel stainless and shining.

elements.name: Manganese
elements.note: Used in steel, batteries, and fertilisers.

elements.name: Iron
elements.note: The most used metal in the world: bridges, tools, and the red cells of blood.

elements.name: Cobalt
elements.note: A hard metal used in magnets, batteries, and blue glass.

elements.name: Nickel
elements.note: A metal used in coins, batteries, and stainless steel.

elements.name: Copper
elements.note: The metal of wires and pipes; it has carried electricity since the first telegraph.

elements.name: Zinc
elements.note: Used to coat steel against rust and to help the body heal.

elements.name: Gallium
elements.note: A metal that melts in the hand; used in LEDs and solar cells.

elements.name: Germanium
elements.note: A metalloid used in fibre-optic cables and infrared lenses.

elements.name: Arsenic
elements.note: A metalloid once used in medicines and dyes; poisonous in larger amounts.

elements.name: Selenium
elements.note: Used in solar cells, copiers, and shampoos.

elements.name: Bromine
elements.note: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; a brown, sharp liquid.

elements.name: Krypton
elements.note: A noble gas used in camera flashes and airport lamps.

elements.name: Rubidium
elements.note: A soft metal used in atomic clocks, the most exact timekeepers.

elements.name: Strontium
elements.note: Used in fireworks for a red colour and in X-ray contrast meals.

elements.name: Yttrium
elements.note: Used in LEDs, lasers, and superconducting magnets.

elements.name: Zirconium
elements.note: A rust-proof metal used in nuclear fuel rods and jewellery.

elements.name: Niobium
elements.note: Used in superconducting magnets and jet engines.

elements.name: Molybdenum
elements.note: A metal that strengthens steel and helps plants fix nitrogen.

elements.name: Technetium
elements.note: Made, not found in nature; used in medical scans.

elements.name: Ruthenium
elements.note: A hard metal used in electrical contacts and fountain-pen nibs.

elements.name: Rhodium
elements.note: A rare metal used in catalytic converters and jewellery.

elements.name: Palladium
elements.note: A metal that soaks up hydrogen; used in catalytic converters.

elements.name: Silver
elements.note: The best carrier of electricity of any metal; used in mirrors, coins, and circuits.

elements.name: Cadmium
elements.note: A soft metal once used in batteries and paints; poisonous, now little used.

elements.name: Indium
elements.note: A soft metal used in touchscreens and solders.

elements.name: Tin
elements.note: The metal of tin cans, solder, and bronze.

elements.name: Antimony
elements.note: A metalloid used in flame-proofing and alloys.

elements.name: Tellurium
elements.note: A metalloid used in solar cells and copiers.

elements.name: Iodine
elements.note: Used to test for starch, to treat thyroids, and in disinfectants.

elements.name: Xenon
elements.note: A noble gas used in car headlamps and projectors.

elements.name: Caesium
elements.note: A soft metal used in atomic clocks and photoelectric cells.

elements.name: Barium
elements.note: A heavy metal used in X-ray meals and green fireworks.

elements.name: Lanthanum
elements.note: The first lanthanide; used in camera lenses and batteries.

elements.name: Cerium
elements.note: Used in flints, glass polishing, and catalytic converters.

elements.name: Praseodymium
elements.note: Used in aircraft magnets and yellow glass.

elements.name: Neodymium
elements.note: Used in magnets, lasers, and the glass of welders' goggles.

elements.name: Promethium
elements.note: Made, not found; once used in glowing paint and nuclear batteries.

elements.name: Samarium
elements.note: Used in magnets, lasers, and the control rods of reactors.

elements.name: Europium
elements.note: Makes the red in television and computer screens.

elements.name: Gadolinium
elements.note: Used in magnets, X-ray contrast, and computer memory.

elements.name: Terbium
elements.note: Used in green phosphors and solid-state devices.

elements.name: Dysprosium
elements.note: Used in magnets, lasers, and data storage.

elements.name: Holmium
elements.note: Used in lasers and in magnets for medical scanners.

elements.name: Erbium
elements.note: Used in pink glass, lasers, and optical fibres.

elements.name: Thulium
elements.note: Used in lasers and in X-ray machines.

elements.name: Ytterbium
elements.note: Used in lasers, atomic clocks, and memory devices.

elements.name: Lutetium
elements.note: Used in medical scanners and in the targets of physics experiments.

elements.name: Hafnium
elements.note: A metal used in nuclear control rods and lamp filaments.

elements.name: Tantalum
elements.note: A metal used in phone parts, jet engines, and surgical tools.

elements.name: Tungsten
elements.note: The metal of light-bulb filaments and cutting tools; it melts hotter than any other metal.

elements.name: Rhenium
elements.note: One of the rarest metals; used in jet engines and thermocouples.

elements.name: Osmium
elements.note: The densest metal; used in fountain-pen nibs and electrical contacts.

elements.name: Iridium
elements.note: A rare metal used in spark plugs and crucibles.

elements.name: Platinum
elements.note: A precious metal used in jewellery, catalytic converters, and fuel cells.

elements.name: Gold
elements.note: The metal of coins, jewellery, and phone contacts; it never corrodes.

elements.name: Mercury
elements.note: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature; once used in thermometers, now little used.

elements.name: Thallium
elements.note: A soft, poisonous metal once used in rat poison and electronics.

elements.name: Lead
elements.note: A heavy, soft metal used in batteries, shields, and weights.

elements.name: Bismuth
elements.note: A metal used in stomach medicines and low-melting alloys.

elements.name: Polonium
elements.note: A rare, radioactive metal that gives off heat; used in space heaters.

elements.name: Astatine
elements.note: The rarest natural element on Earth; almost nothing is known of it.

elements.name: Radon
elements.note: A radioactive noble gas that seeps from rocks; houses are tested for it.

elements.name: Francium
elements.note: A rare, radioactive alkali metal that vanishes in minutes.

elements.name: Radium
elements.note: A radioactive metal once used in glowing paint and cancer treatment.

elements.name: Actinium
elements.note: The first actinide; used in research and as a parent of later elements.

elements.name: Thorium
elements.note: A radioactive metal that may fuel future power stations.

elements.name: Protactinium
elements.note: A rare, radioactive metal found in uranium ores.

elements.name: Uranium
elements.note: The fuel of nuclear power stations and the heaviest natural element.

elements.name: Neptunium
elements.note: Made, not found; used in smoke detectors and research.

elements.name: Plutonium
elements.note: Made for nuclear power and weapons research; it exists in tiny amounts in nature.

elements.name: Americium
elements.note: Used in smoke detectors and in the power of deep-space probes.

elements.name: Curium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; used in research and in neutron sources.

elements.name: Berkelium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the city of Berkeley.

elements.name: Californium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the state of California.

elements.name: Einsteinium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Albert Einstein.

elements.name: Fermium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Enrico Fermi.

elements.name: Mendelevium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Dmitri Mendeleev.

elements.name: Nobelium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Alfred Nobel.

elements.name: Lawrencium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Ernest Lawrence.

elements.name: Rutherfordium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Ernest Rutherford.

elements.name: Dubnium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Dubna, in Russia.

elements.name: Seaborgium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Glenn Seaborg.

elements.name: Bohrium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Niels Bohr.

elements.name: Hassium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the state of Hesse, in Germany.

elements.name: Meitnerium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Lise Meitner.

elements.name: Darmstadtium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the city of Darmstadt.

elements.name: Roentgenium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Wilhelm Röntgen.

elements.name: Copernicium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Nicolaus Copernicus.

elements.name: Nihonium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Japan (Nihon).

elements.name: Flerovium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the Flerov Laboratory.

elements.name: Moscovium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Moscow Oblast.

elements.name: Livermorium
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the Lawrence Livermore Laboratory.

elements.name: Tennessine
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for the state of Tennessee.

elements.name: Oganesson
elements.note: Made in laboratories; named for Yuri Oganessian. Only a handful of atoms have ever existed.

source: The live Periodic Elements Database (118 records); masses for laboratory-made elements are the whole numbers of their longest-lived forms.
